content: Brood parasites are organisms that engage in a reproductive strategy known as brood parasitism, a form of kleptoparasitism observed in birds, fish, and insects. This strategy involves manipulating and exploiting host individuals, either of the same species (intraspecific brood parasitism) or different species (interspecific brood parasitism), to raise the offspring of the parasitic organism. By doing so, the parasitic parent avoids the energetic costs of rearing young or building nests, allowing them to allocate more time and resources to foraging, producing additional offspring, and other activities. In many monogamous bird species, extra-pair matings occur, where males outside the pair bond sire offspring. This behavior allows males to evade the parental investment required to raise their offspring. This form of cuckoldry is further extended when females lay their eggs in the nests of other individuals. Intraspecific brood parasitism is observed in several duck species, such as the Goldeneye (Bucephala clangula), where females lay their eggs in the nests of other females. Interspecific brood parasites include Old World cuckoos in Eurasia and Australia, cowbirds and Black-headed Ducks in the Americas, and indigobirds, whydahs, and honeyguides in Africa. Most avian brood parasites are specialists, targeting a single host species or a small group of closely related host species. However, some, like four of the five parasitic cowbird species, are generalists, parasitizing a wide variety of hosts. For instance, the Brown-headed Cowbird has been documented to parasitize 221 different host species. Typically, brood parasites lay only one egg per host nest, although in some cases, such as with cowbirds, multiple females may use the same host nest. The Common Cuckoo presents an interesting case where the species as a whole parasitizes a wide range of hosts, but individual females specialize in a single host species. Genes regulating egg coloration are maternally inherited, enabling females to lay eggs that mimic those of their specific host species. Female cuckoos are thought to imprint on the host species that raised them and subsequently parasitize nests of that species. Male Common Cuckoos, however, fertilize females from all maternal lines, ensuring sufficient gene flow between different maternal lines. The mechanisms by which female cuckoos select their hosts remain unclear, but hypotheses include genetic inheritance of host preference, host imprinting during development, natal philopatry (returning to the place of birth and choosing a host randomly), nest-site preference, and habitat preference. Experimental evidence has most strongly supported the nest-site and habitat-selection hypotheses. Specialist avian brood parasites often exhibit adaptations such as mimetic eggs, which closely resemble the eggs of their host species. There is evidence suggesting that even generalist parasites like the Brown-headed Cowbird may have evolved egg coloration that mimics those of their hosts. Most avian brood parasites remove a host egg when laying their own in the nest. This behavior may occur during the same visit to the host nest or during a separate visit before or after parasitism. The removal of a host egg may serve to prevent the host from recognizing that its nest has been parasitized or to reduce competition for resources once the parasitic chick hatches. Brood parasites typically have short egg incubation periods and rapid nestling growth, giving their chicks a competitive advantage over host nestlings. In cases where host nestlings are significantly smaller than the parasitic chick, the host nestlings often starve to death. Some brood parasites eliminate their nestmates shortly after hatching, either by ejecting them from the nest or killing them using sharp mandibular hooks, which fall off after a few days. The Mafia hypothesis seeks to explain why many host species care for the nestlings of brood parasites, despite the significant costs to their own reproductive success. This hypothesis suggests that brood parasites manipulate their hosts through aggressive behaviors. If a host detects and rejects a parasitic egg, the parasite may retaliate by destroying the host's nest, injuring or killing its nestlings, and reducing the host's reproductive success. This threatening behavior creates selective pressures that favor compliance by the host, leading to a feedback loop between aggressive parasite behavior and host compliance. Two avian species, the Brown-headed Cowbird (Molothrus ater) of North America and the Great Spotted Cuckoo (Clamator glandarius) of Europe, have been observed to exhibit Mafia-like behavior. The Great Spotted Cuckoo primarily parasitizes the nests of the European Magpie (Pica pica) and has been observed to repeatedly visit parasitized nests, a behavior consistent with the Mafia hypothesis. An experiment conducted by Soler et al. from 1990 to 1992 in Spain examined the effects of removing cuckoo eggs on the reproductive success of magpies. The researchers found that nests from which parasitic eggs were removed were depredated at much higher rates than those where the eggs were left intact. Using plasticine eggs to model magpie eggs, they confirmed that the nest destruction was caused by the Great Spotted Cuckoo. This destruction benefits the cuckoo, as the possibility of the magpie re-nesting provides another opportunity for the cuckoo to parasitize the new nest. A similar experiment conducted by Hoover et al. from 1996 to 2002 studied the relationship between the parasitic Brown-headed Cowbird and its host, the Prothonotary Warbler (Protonotaria citrea). They found that 56% of nests from which cowbird eggs were ejected were depredated, compared to only 6% of nests where the eggs were accepted. Among rebuilt nests of previously depredated hosts, 85% were destroyed. Hosts that ejected cowbird eggs produced 60% fewer young compared to those that accepted the parasitic eggs. Although limited experimentation has been conducted to test the Mafia hypothesis, these studies provide compelling evidence. Host species have evolved various defenses against brood parasitism to mitigate its detrimental effects on their reproductive success. The most effective defense is to avoid parasitism altogether, which can be achieved by selecting nest sites that are difficult for parasites to access, beginning incubation early to guard the nest during parasite visits, and aggressively defending their territory. Birds nesting in groups may also benefit from collective defense. Once parasitism has occurred, the next best defense is to eject the parasitic egg, either by grasping it with a large enough beak or by puncturing it. However, egg ejection carries risks, especially when dealing with mimetic eggs. Hosts may mistakenly eject one of their own eggs or damage their eggs while attempting to remove a parasitic egg. Some hosts that do not exhibit egg ejection behavior may abandon parasitized nests and start anew, although this strategy becomes maladaptive at high parasitism rates, as the new nest is likely to be re-parasitized. Insects also exhibit brood parasitism. Cuckoo bees, for example, lay their eggs in the nest cells of other bees. These insects are often referred to as kleptoparasites rather than brood parasites. Similarly, cuckoo wasps lay their eggs in the nests of potter and mud dauber wasps, among others. Various lineages of wasps across different families have independently evolved similar parasitic behaviors.
